newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries open higher, dollar strength cited.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries open higher, dollar strength cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened firm on Monday, aided by a stronger dollar, analysts said.
"The main story is the dollar has been firmer," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A.
In early trade, the benchmark 30-year bond was up 5/32 to 94-01, yielding 7.11 percent.

The dollar reached a 50-month peak against the yen in early U.S. trade and traded above 1.70 marks, with interest rate differentials and Japanese capital outflows viewed as the driving forces behind the strength.
Facing a light calendar of economic news on Monday, analysts said Treasuries would watch the foreign exchange markets and the U.S. equity market.
"It's a pretty light calendar," said Sloan. "Consumer credit and (manufacturers' and retailers' fourth-quarter) profits are not market movers."
The Treasury will sell $13.0 billion in three- and six-month bills at its weekly bill auction at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT, a routine event that is expected to proceed smoothly.
On Tuesday, the Treasury will sell $8.0 billion in 10-year index-linked bonds.
Economic data will grow in importance for the market toward the end of the week, analysts said.
On Friday, the government will report March producer price and retail sales data.

According to a Reuters poll, the Producer Price Index (PPI) is expected to be unchanged after falling 0.4 percent in February. March retail sales are expected to be up 0.6 percent after rising 0.8 percent in February.
The retail sales data, especially, are of great interest to the market since the Federal Reserve is closely monitoring the demand side of the economy.

After yields rose and prices fell on Friday in response to a strong March employment report, resistance in the June bond contract is seen at 107-17 and support is gathered below 106-25, analysts said.
Resistance for the 30-year cash bond yield is seen at seven percent with support seen emerging as the yield nears 7.15 percent.
"There's support for the bond yield at 7-1/8 percent," said Kevin Flanagan. "We're in a tight band right now, especially since this March employment report."
"Except for the payroll jobs growth number, the employment report was strong," said Flanagan. "The Fed's going to have to tighten."
The spread between the two- and 30-year bond was at 69 basis points in early dealings. But Flanagan said the vulnerable part of the maturity curve is the front end.
"If you believe Fed funds are going to six percent, you have a lot of ground to make up because you have not factored in that type of a move," he said.
In the bill sector, three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.15 percent.
Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.29 percent and the year bill rate was down one basis point to 5.63 percent.
In other key issues, the five-year note traded up 2/32 to 99-16/32 to yield 6.74 percent, and the 10-year was up 3/32 to 95-15/32 to yield 6.89 percent.
(( -- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
